Amplitude envelope attack time: Specifies how long it takes for the sound to reach its peak value, relative to the onset.

Sets the Frequency Modulation Harmonicity Ratio. Controls the timbre of the sound. Whole numbers and simple ratios sound more natural, while decimal numbers and complex ratios sound metallic. A number may be added afterwards to control the harmonicity of any of the 8 individual FMs (e.g. fmh2)
x:
note("c e g b g e")
.fm(4)
.fmh("<1 2 1.5 1.61>")
._scope()

entries.d: Sets the Frequency Modulation of the synth. Controls the modulation index, which defines the brightness of the sound. A number may be added afterwards to control the modulation index of any of the 8 individual FMs (e.g. fm3). Also, FMs may be routed into each other with matrix commands like fm13, which would send fm1 back into fm3
x:
note("c e g b g e")
.fm("<0 1 2 8 32>")
._scope()

entries.d: Ramp type of fm envelope. Exp might be a bit broken.. A number may be added afterwards to control the envelope of any of the 8 individual FMs (e.g. fmenv4)
x:
note("c e g b g e")
.fm(4)
.fmdecay(.2)
.fmsustain(0)
.fmenv("<exp lin>")
._scope()

entries.d: Attack time for the FM envelope: time it takes to reach maximum modulation A number may be added afterwards to control the attack of the envelope of any of the 8 individual FMs (e.g. fmatt5)
x:
note("c e g b g e")
.fm(4)
.fmattack("<0 .05 .1 .2>")
._scope()

entries.d: Waveform of the fm modulator A number may be added afterwards to control the waveform any of the 8 individual FMs (e.g. fmwave6)

Decay time for the FM envelope: seconds until the sustain level is reached after the attack phase. A number may be added afterwards to control the decay of the envelope of any of the 8 individual FMs (e.g. fmdec6)
x:
note("c e g b g e")
.fm(4)
.fmdecay("<.01 .05 .1 .2>")
.fmsustain(.4)
._scope()

entries.d: Sustain level for the FM envelope: how much modulation is applied after the decay phase A number may be added afterwards to control the sustain of the envelope of any of the 8 individual FMs (e.g. fmsus7)
x:
note("c e g b g e")
.fm(4)
.fmdecay(.1)
.fmsustain("<1 .75 .5 0>")
._scope()

entries.d: Release time for the FM envelope: how much modulation is applied after the note is released A number may be added afterwards to control the release of the envelope of any of the 8 individual FMs (e.g. fmrel8)

entries.d: Used in conjunction with speed, accepts values of "r" (rate, default behavior), "c" (cycles), or "s" (seconds). Using unit "c" means speed will be interpreted in units of cycles, e.g. speed "1" means samples will be stretched to fill a cycle. Using unit "s" means the playback speed will be adjusted so that the duration is the number of seconds specified by speed.

Made by Calum Gunn. Reminiscent of some weird mixture of filter, ring-modulator and pitch-shifter. The SuperCollider manual defines Squiz as: "A simplistic pitch-raising algorithm. It's not meant to sound natural; its sound is reminiscent of some weird mixture of filter, ring-modulator and pitch-shifter, depending on the input. The algorithm works by cutting the signal into fragments (delimited by upwards-going zero-crossings) and squeezing those fragments in the time domain (i.e. simply playing them back faster than they came in), leaving silences inbetween. All the parameters apart from memlen can be modulated."
p: Try passing multiples of 2 to it - 2, 4, 8 etc.

Configures an LFO. Can be called in sequence like pat.lfo(...).lfo(...) to set up multiple LFOs. There are two ways to declare which control will be modulated: Explicitly put control in the config (e.g. lfo({ c: "lpf" })) If the control parameter is absent, the control immediately before the lfo call will be used (e.g. s("saw").lpf(500).lfo() to modulate lpf) Modulators can be referred to by id so that they can be updated later e.g. inside a sometimes. See example below.

entries.d: Changes the structure of the pattern to form an Euclidean rhythm. Euclidean rhythms are rhythms obtained using the greatest common divisor of two numbers. They were described in 2004 by Godfried Toussaint, a Canadian computer scientist. Euclidean rhythms are really useful for computer/algorithmic music because they can describe a large number of rhythms with a couple of numbers.
p: the number of steps to fill

entries.d: Similar to euclid, but each pulse is held until the next pulse, so there will be no gaps.

entries.d: Similar to euclid, but each pulse is held until the next pulse, so there will be no gaps, and has an additional parameter for 'rotating' the resulting sequence

entries.d: A 'euclid' variant with an additional parameter that morphs the resulting rhythm from 0 (no morphing) to 1 (completely 'even'). For example sound("bd").euclidish(3,8,0) would be the same as sound("bd").euclid(3,8), and sound("bd").euclidish(3,8,1) would be the same as sound("bd bd bd"). sound("bd").euclidish(3,8,0.5) would have a groove somewhere between. Inspired by the work of Malcom Braff.
p: the number of steps to fill
exists between the extremes of 0 (straight euclidian) and 1 (straight pulse)

Assumes a pattern of numbers. Adds the given number to each item in the pattern.
Like add, but the given numbers are subtracted.
x:
n("0 2 4".sub("<0 1 2 3>")).scale("C4:minor")
// See add for more information.

entries.d: Multiplies each number by the given factor.
Divides each number by the given factor.
Applies the given structure to the pattern:
x:
note("c,eb,g")
  .struct("x ~ x ~ ~ x ~ x ~ ~ ~ x ~ x ~ ~")
  .slow(2)

entries.d: Returns silence when mask is 0 or "~"
Does absolutely nothing, but with a given metrical 'steps'
Does absolutely nothing..
A discrete value that repeats once per cycle.
The given items are played at the same time at the same length.
Concatenation: combines a list of patterns, switching between them successively, one per cycle.
The given items are concatenated, where each one takes one cycle.
Allows to arrange multiple patterns together over multiple cycles. Takes a variable number of arrays with two elements specifying the number of cycles and the pattern to use.
See fastcat
Like cat, but the items are crammed into one cycle.
Registers a new pattern method. The method is added to the Pattern class + the standalone function is returned from register.
p: name of the function, or an array of names to be used as synonyms
function with 1 or more params, where last is the current pattern
defaults to true; if set to false, you will have more control over the arguments to func as they will be in their raw form and it will be up to you to patternify them and/or query them for values

entries.d: Assumes a numerical pattern. Returns a new pattern with all values rounded to the nearest integer.
Assumes a numerical pattern. Returns a new pattern with all values set to their mathematical floor. E.g. 3.7 replaced with to 3, and -4.2 replaced with -5.
Assumes a numerical pattern. Returns a new pattern with all values set to their mathematical ceiling. E.g. 3.2 replaced with 4, and -4.2 replaced with -4.
Assumes a numerical pattern, containing unipolar values in the range 0 .. Returns a new pattern with values scaled to the bipolar range -1 .. 1
Assumes a numerical pattern, containing bipolar values in the range -1 .. 1 Returns a new pattern with values scaled to the unipolar range 0 .. 1
Assumes a numerical pattern, containing unipolar values in the range 0 .. 1. Returns a new pattern with values scaled to the given min/max range. Most useful in combination with continuous patterns.
Assumes a numerical pattern, containing unipolar values in the range 0 .. 1 Returns a new pattern with values scaled to the given min/max range, following an exponential curve.
Assumes a numerical pattern, containing bipolar values in the range -1 .. 1 Returns a new pattern with values scaled to the given min/max range.
Allows dividing numbers via list notation using ":". Returns a new pattern with just numbers.
Compress each cycle into the given timespan, leaving a gap
x:
cat(
  s("bd sd").compress(.25,.75),
  s("~ bd sd ~")
)

entries.d: speeds up a pattern like fast, but rather than it playing multiple times as fast would it instead leaves a gap in the remaining space of the cycle. For example, the following will play the sound pattern "bd sn" only once but compressed into the first half of the cycle, i.e. twice as fast.
Similar to compress, but doesn't leave gaps, and the 'focus' can be bigger than a cycle
The ply function repeats each event the given number of times.
Speed up a pattern by the given factor. Used by "*" in mini notation.
x: s("bd hh sd hh").fast(2) // s("[bd hh sd hh]*2")

entries.d: Both speeds up the pattern (like 'fast') and the sample playback (like 'speed').
Slow down a pattern over the given number of cycles. Like the "/" operator in mini notation.
x: s("bd hh sd hh").slow(2) // s("[bd hh sd hh]/2")

entries.d: Carries out an operation 'inside' a cycle.
Carries out an operation 'outside' a cycle.
Applies the given function every n cycles, starting from the last cycle.
Applies the given function every n cycles, starting from the first cycle.
An alias for firstOf
Like layer, but with a single function:
Plays the pattern at the given cycles per minute.
Nudge a pattern to start earlier in time. Equivalent of Tidal's <~ operator
p: number of cycles to nudge left

entries.d: Nudge a pattern to start later in time. Equivalent of Tidal's ~> operator
p: number of cycles to nudge right

entries.d: Plays a portion of a pattern, specified by the beginning and end of a time span. The new resulting pattern is played over the time period of the original pattern:
x:
s("bd*2 hh*3 [sd bd]*2 perc").zoom(0.25, 0.75)
// s("hh*3 [sd bd]*2") // equivalent

entries.d: Splits a pattern into the given number of slices, and plays them according to a pattern of slice numbers. Similar to slice, but slices up patterns rather than sound samples.
Selects the given fraction of the pattern and repeats that part to fill the remainder of the cycle.
Samples the pattern at a rate of n events per cycle. Useful for turning a continuous pattern into a discrete one.

The function swingBy x n breaks each cycle into n slices, and then delays events in the second half of each slice by the amount x, which is relative to the size of the (half) slice. So if x is 0 it does nothing, 0.5 delays for half the note duration, and 1 will wrap around to doing nothing again. The end result is a shuffle or swing-like rhythm
Shorthand for swingBy with 1/3:
Swaps 1s and 0s in a binary pattern.
Applies the given function whenever the given pattern is in a true state.
Superimposes the function result on top of the original pattern, delayed by the given time.
Returns a new pattern where every other cycle is played once, twice as fast, and offset in time by one quarter of a cycle. Creates a kind of breakbeat feel.
Reverse all cycles in a pattern. See also revv for reversing a whole pattern.
Reverse a whole pattern. See also rev for reversing each cycle.
Like press, but allows you to specify the amount by which each event is shifted. pressBy(0.5) is the same as press, while pressBy(1/3) shifts each event by a third of its timespan.
Syncopates a rhythm, by shifting each event halfway into its timespan.
Silences a pattern.
Applies rev to a pattern every other cycle, so that the pattern alternates between forwards and backwards.
Jux with adjustable stereo width. 0 = mono, 1 = full stereo.
x: s("bd lt [~ ht] mt cp ~ bd hh").juxBy("<0 .5 1>/2", rev)

entries.d: The jux function creates strange stereo effects, by applying a function to a pattern, but only in the right-hand channel.
x: s("bd lt [~ ht] mt cp ~ bd hh").jux(rev)
s("bd lt [~ ht] mt cp ~ bd hh").jux(press)
s("bd lt [~ ht] mt cp ~ bd hh").jux(iter(4))

entries.d: Superimpose and offset multiple times, applying the given function each time.
p: function to apply, given the pattern and the iteration index

entries.d: Superimpose and offset multiple times, gradually decreasing the velocity
Deprecated. Like echo, but the last 2 parameters are flipped.
The plyWith function repeats each event the given number of times, applying the given function to each event.\n
p: function to apply, given the pattern

entries.d: The plyForEach function repeats each event the given number of times, applying the given function to each event. This version of ply uses the iteration index as an argument to the function, similar to echoWith.
p: function to apply, given the pattern and the iteration index

entries.d: Divides a pattern into a given number of subdivisions, plays the subdivisions in order, but increments the starting subdivision each cycle. The pattern wraps to the first subdivision after the last subdivision is played.
Like iter, but plays the subdivisions in reverse order. Known as iter' in tidalcycles
Repeats each cycle the given number of times.
Divides a pattern into a given number of parts, then cycles through those parts in turn, applying the given function to each part in turn (one part per cycle).
Like chunk, but cycles through the parts in reverse order. Known as chunk' in tidalcycles
Like chunk, but the cycles of the source pattern aren't repeated for each set of chunks.
Like chunk, but the function is applied to a looped subcycle of the source pattern.
x:
sound("bd sd ht lt bd - cp lt").chunkInto(4, hurry(2))
  .bank("tr909")

entries.d: Like chunkInto, but moves backwards through the chunks.
x:
sound("bd sd ht lt bd - cp lt").chunkInto(4, hurry(2))
  .bank("tr909")

entries.d: Loops the pattern inside an offset for cycles. If you think of the entire span of time in cycles as a ribbon, you can cut a single piece and loop it.
p: start point of loop in cycles

entries.d: Use within to apply a function to only a part of a pattern.
p: end within cycle (0 - 1). Must be > start
function to be applied to the sub-pattern

entries.d: Experimental Speeds a pattern up or down, to fit to the given number of steps per cycle.
x:
sound("bd sd cp").pace(4)
// The same as sound("{bd sd cp}%4") or sound("<bd sd cp>*4")

entries.d: Experimental Aligns the steps of the patterns, creating polymeters. The patterns are repeated until they all fit the cycle. For example, in the below the first pattern is repeated twice, and the second is repeated three times, to fit the lowest common multiple of six steps.
x:
// The same as note("{c eb g, c2 g2}%6")
polymeter("c eb g", "c2 g2").note()

entries.d: 'Concatenates' patterns like fastcat, but proportional to a number of steps per cycle. The steps can either be inferred from the pattern, or provided as a [length, pattern] pair. Has the alias timecat.
x:
stepcat("bd sd cp","hh hh").sound()
// the same as "bd sd cp hh hh".sound()

entries.d: Experimental Concatenates patterns stepwise, according to an inferred 'steps per cycle'. Similar to stepcat, but if an argument is a list, the whole pattern will alternate between the elements in the list.
x:
stepalt(["bd cp", "mt"], "bd").sound()
// The same as "bd cp bd mt bd".sound()

entries.d: Experimental Takes the given number of steps from a pattern (dropping the rest). A positive number will take steps from the start of a pattern, and a negative number from the end.
x:
"bd cp ht mt".take("2").sound()
// The same as "bd cp".sound()

"bd cp ht mt".take("1 2 3").sound()
// The same as "bd bd cp bd cp ht".sound()

"bd cp ht mt".take("-1 -2 -3").sound()
// The same as "mt ht mt cp ht mt".sound()

entries.d: Experimental Drops the given number of steps from a pattern. A positive number will drop steps from the start of a pattern, and a negative number from the end.

Experimental extend is similar to fast in that it increases its density, but it also increases the step count accordingly. So stepcat("a b".extend(2), "c d") would be the same as "a b a b c d", whereas stepcat("a b".fast(2), "c d") would be the same as "[a b] [a b] c d".
x:
stepcat(
  sound("bd bd - cp").extend(2),
  sound("bd - sd -")
).pace(8)

entries.d: Experimental replicate is similar to fast in that it increases its density, but it also increases the step count accordingly. So stepcat("a b".replicate(2), "c d") would be the same as "a b a b c d", whereas stepcat("a b".fast(2), "c d") would be the same as "[a b] [a b] c d". TODO: find out how this function differs from extend
x:
stepcat(
  sound("bd bd - cp").replicate(2),
  sound("bd - sd -")
).pace(8)

entries.d: Experimental Expands the step size of the pattern by the given factor.
Experimental Contracts the step size of the pattern by the given factor. See also expand.

Experimental Progressively shrinks the pattern by 'n' steps until there's nothing left, or if a second value is given (using mininotation list syntax with :), that number of times. A positive number will progressively drop steps from the start of a pattern, and a negative number from the end.

Experimental Progressively grows the pattern by 'n' steps until the full pattern is played, or if a second value is given (using mininotation list syntax with :), that number of times. A positive number will progressively grow steps from the start of a pattern, and a negative number from the end.

Experimental Inserts a pattern into a list of patterns. On the first repetition it will be inserted at the end of the list, then moved backwards through the list on successive repetitions. The patterns are added together stepwise, with all repetitions taking place over a single cycle. Using pace to set the number of steps per cycle is therefore usually recommended.
x:
"[c g]".tour("e f", "e f g", "g f e c").note()
   .sound("folkharp")
   .pace(8)

entries.d: Experimental 'zips' together the steps of the provided patterns. This can create a long repetition, taking place over a single, dense cycle. Using pace to set the number of steps per cycle is therefore usually recommended.
x:
zip("e f", "e f g", "g [f e] a f4 c").note()
   .sound("folkharp")
   .pace(8)

entries.d: Aliases for stepcat
Cuts each sample into the given number of parts, allowing you to explore a technique known as 'granular synthesis'. It turns a pattern of samples into a pattern of parts of samples.
x:
samples({ rhodes: 'https://cdn.freesound.org/previews/132/132051_316502-lq.mp3' })
s("rhodes")
 .chop(4)
 .rev() // reverse order of chops
 .loopAt(2) // fit sample into 2 cycles

entries.d: Cuts each sample into the given number of parts, triggering progressive portions of each sample at each loop.
Makes the sample fit the given number of cycles by changing the speed.

Chops samples into the given number of slices, triggering those slices with a given pattern of slice numbers. Instead of a number, it also accepts a list of numbers from 0 to 1 to slice at specific points.
make something happen on event time uses browser timeout which is innacurate for audio tasks
Works the same as slice, but changes the playback speed of each slice to match the duration of its step.
Makes the sample fit its event duration. Good for rhythmical loops like drum breaks. Similar to loopAt.
Makes the sample fit the given number of cycles and cps value, by changing the speed. Please note that at some point cps will be given by a global clock and this function will be deprecated/removed.
Cross-fades between left and right from 0 to 1: 0 = (full left, no right) .5 = (both equal) 1 = (no left, full right)
creates a structure pattern from divisions of a cycle especially useful for creating rhythms
Takes two binary rhythms represented as lists of 1s and 0s, and a number between 0 and 1 that morphs between them. The two lists should contain the same number of true values.
Soft-clipping distortion
Hard-clipping distortion
Cubic polynomial distortion
Diode-emulating distortion
Asymmetrical diode distortion
Wavefolding distortion
Wavefolding distortion composed with sinusoid
Distortion via Chebyshev polynomials
Scale the magnitude of the harmonics of one of the core synths ('sine', 'tri', 'saw', ..) Can also be used to create a new synth via s('user').partials(...)
p: List of [0, 1] magnitudes for partials. 0th entry is the fundamental harmonic (i.e. DC offset is skipped)

entries.d: Rotates the harmonics of one of the core synths ('sine', 'tri', 'saw', 'user', ..) by a list of phases
p: List of [0, 1) phases for partials. 0th entry is the fundamental phase (i.e. DC offset is skipped)

entries.d: Picks patterns (or plain values) either from a list (by index) or a lookup table (by name). Similar to inhabit, but maintains the structure of the original patterns.
x: note("<0 1 2!2 3>".pick(["g a", "e f", "f g f g" , "g c d"]))

entries.d: The same as pick, but if you pick a number greater than the size of the list, it wraps around, rather than sticking at the maximum value. For example, if you pick the fifth pattern of a list of three, you'll get the second one.
pickF lets you use a pattern of numbers to pick which function to apply to another pattern.
p: the array of functions from which to pull

entries.d: The same as pickF, but if you pick a number greater than the size of the functions list, it wraps around, rather than sticking at the maximum value.
p: the array of functions from which to pull

entries.d: Similar to pick, but it applies an outerJoin instead of an innerJoin.
The same as pickOut, but if you pick a number greater than the size of the list, it wraps around, rather than sticking at the maximum value.
Similar to pick, but the choosen pattern is restarted when its index is triggered.
The same as pickRestart, but if you pick a number greater than the size of the list, it wraps around, rather than sticking at the maximum value.
Similar to pick, but the choosen pattern is reset when its index is triggered.
The same as pickReset, but if you pick a number greater than the size of the list, it wraps around, rather than sticking at the maximum value.
Picks patterns (or plain values) either from a list (by index) or a lookup table (by name). Similar to pick, but cycles are squeezed into the target ('inhabited') pattern.

The same as inhabit, but if you pick a number greater than the size of the list, it wraps around, rather than sticking at the maximum value. For example, if you pick the fifth pattern of a list of three, you'll get the second one.
Pick from the list of values (or patterns of values) via the index using the given pattern of integers. The selected pattern will be compressed to fit the duration of the selecting event
x: note(squeeze("<0@2 [1!2] 2>", ["g a", "f g f g" , "g a c d"]))

entries.d: Changes the global tempo to the given cycles per minute

Applies a function to each of the running patterns separately. This is intended for future use with upcoming 'stepwise' features. See all for a version that applies the function to all the patterns stacked together into a single pattern. $: sound("bd - cp sd") $: sound("hh*8") each(fast("<2 3>"))
A sawtooth signal between 0 and 1.
A sawtooth signal between -1 and 1 (like saw, but bipolar).
A sawtooth signal between 1 and 0 (like saw, but flipped).
A sawtooth signal between 1 and -1 (like saw2, but flipped).
A sine signal between -1 and 1 (like sine, but bipolar).
A sine signal between 0 and 1.
A cosine signal between 0 and 1.
A cosine signal between -1 and 1 (like cosine, but bipolar).
A square signal between 0 and 1.
A square signal between -1 and 1 (like square, but bipolar).
A triangle signal between 0 and 1.
A triangle signal between -1 and 1 (like tri, but bipolar).
An inverted triangle signal between 1 and 0 (like tri, but flipped).
An inverted triangle signal between -1 and 1 (like itri, but bipolar).
A signal representing the cycle time.
The mouse's x position value ranges from 0 to 1.
The mouse's y position value ranges from 0 to 1.
A discrete pattern of numbers from 0 to n-1
Creates a binary pattern from a number.
p: input number to convert to binary

entries.d: Creates a binary pattern from a number, padded to n bits long.
p: input number to convert to binary

entries.d: Creates a binary list pattern from a number.
p: input number to convert to binary s("saw").seg(8) .partials(binaryL(irand(4096).add(1)))

entries.d: Creates a binary list pattern from a number, padded to n bits long.
p: input number to convert to binary

entries.d: Creates a list of random numbers of the given length
p: Number of random numbers to sample

entries.d: Slices a pattern into the given number of parts, then plays those parts in random order. Each part will be played exactly once per cycle.
Slices a pattern into the given number of parts, then plays those parts at random. Similar to shuffle, but parts might be played more than once, or not at all, per cycle.
Modify a pattern by applying a function to the randomSeed control if present
p: Function from seed (or undefined) to seed (or undefined)

entries.d: Change the seed for random signals. Normally, random signals depend on time, so two patterns at the same time will have the same random values. Specifying a new seed changes the signal output by rand. This also affects other functions that use randomness, like shuffle and sometimes.
p: A new seed. Can be any number.
x:
$: s("hh*4").degrade();
$: s("bd*4").degrade().seed(1); // Will degrade different events from the hi-hat

entries.d: A continuous pattern of random numbers, between 0 and 1.
A continuous pattern of random numbers, between -1 and 1
A continuous pattern of 0 or 1 (binary random), with a probability for the value being 1
A continuous pattern of 0 or 1 (binary random)
A continuous pattern of random integers, between 0 and n-1.
x:
// randomly select scale notes from 0 - 7 (= C to C)
n(irand(8)).struct("x x*2 x x*3").scale("C:minor")

entries.d: Choose from the list of values (or patterns of values) using the given pattern of numbers, which should be in the range of 0..1
As with {chooseWith}, but the structure comes from the chosen values, rather than the pattern you're using to choose with.
Chooses randomly from the given list of elements.
As with choose, but the pattern that this method is called on should be in the range -1 .. 1
Picks one of the elements at random each cycle.
Chooses randomly from the given list of elements by giving a probability to each element
Picks one of the elements at random each cycle by giving a probability to each element
x: wchooseCycles(["c c c",5], ["a a a",3], ["f f f",1]).fast(4).note()

// The probability can itself be a pattern
wchooseCycles(["bd(3,8)","<5 0>"], ["hh hh hh",3]).fast(4).s()

entries.d: Generates a continuous pattern of perlin noise, in the range 0..1.

Generates a continuous pattern of [berlin noise](conceived by Jame Coyne and Jade Rowland as a joke but turned out to be surprisingly cool and useful, like perlin noise but with sawtooth waves), in the range 0..1.
Randomly removes events from the pattern by a given amount. 0 = 0% chance of removal 1 = 100% chance of removal
Randomly removes 50% of events from the pattern. Shorthand for .degradeBy(0.5)

Inverse of degradeBy: Randomly removes events from the pattern by a given amount. 0 = 100% chance of removal 1 = 0% chance of removal Events that would be removed by degradeBy are let through by undegradeBy and vice versa (see second example).

Inverse of degrade: Randomly removes 50% of events from the pattern. Shorthand for .undegradeBy(0.5) Events that would be removed by degrade are let through by undegrade and vice versa (see second example).
Randomly applies the given function by the given probability. Similar to someCyclesBy
Applies the given function with a 50% chance
Randomly applies the given function by the given probability on a cycle by cycle basis. Similar to sometimesBy
Shorthand for .someCyclesBy(0.5, fn)
Shorthand for .sometimesBy(0.75, fn)
Shorthand for .sometimesBy(0.25, fn)
Shorthand for .sometimesBy(0.1, fn)
Shorthand for .sometimesBy(0.9, fn)
Shorthand for .sometimesBy(0, fn) (never calls fn)
Shorthand for .sometimesBy(1, fn) (always calls fn)
Do something on a keypress, or array of keypresses Key name reference
returns true when a key or array of keys is held Key name reference

A pattern measuring the duration of events, in cycles per event. cyclesPer doesn't have structure itself, but takes structure, and therefore event durations, from the pattern that it is combined with. For example cyclesPer.struct("1 1 [1 1] 1") would give the same as "0.25 0.25 [0.125 0.125] 0.25". See also its reciprocal, per, also known as perCycle.
x:
sound("bd sd [bd bd] sd*4 [- sd] [bd [bd bd]]")
  .note(cyclesPer.add(20))

entries.d: A pattern measuring the 'shortness' of events, or in other words, the duration of pattern events, in events per cycle. per doesn't have structure itself, but takes structure, and therefore event durations, from the pattern that it is combined with. For example per.struct("1 1 [1 1] 1") would give the same as "4 4 [8 8] 4". See also its reciprocal, cyclesPer.

Like per but measures the shortness of events according to an exponential curve. In particular, where the event duration halves, the returned value increases by one. perx.struct("1 1 [1 [1 1]] 1") would therefore be the same as "3 3 [4 [5 5]] 3".

Visualises a pattern as a scrolling 'pianoroll', displayed in the background of the editor. To show a pianoroll for all running patterns, use all(pianoroll). To have a pianoroll appear below a pattern instead, prefix with _, e.g.: sound("bd sd")._pianoroll().
p: Object containing all the optional following parameters as key value pairs:
number of cycles to be displayed at the same time - defaults to 4
location of the active notes on the time axis - 0 to 1, defaults to 0.5
displays the roll vertically - 0 by default
displays labels on individual notes (see the label function) - 0 by default
reverse the direction of the roll - 0 by default
reverse the relative location of notes on the value axis - 0 by default
lookup X cycles outside of the cycles window to display notes in advance - 1 by default
hide notes with negative time (before starting playing the pattern) - 0 by default
notes leave a solid trace - 0 by default
notes takes the full value axis width - 0 by default
hexadecimal or CSS color of the active notes - defaults to #FFCA28
hexadecimal or CSS color of the inactive notes - defaults to #7491D2
hexadecimal or CSS color of the background - defaults to transparent
hexadecimal or CSS color of the line representing the play head - defaults to white
notes are filled with color (otherwise only the label is displayed) - 0 by default
active notes are filled with color - 0 by default
notes are shown with colored borders - 0 by default
active notes are shown with colored borders - 0 by default
only active notes are shown - 0 by default
use note color for inactive notes - 1 by default
define the font used by notes labels - defaults to 'monospace'
minimum note value to display on the value axis - defaults to 10
maximum note value to display on the value axis - defaults to 90
automatically calculate the minMidi and maxMidi parameters - 0 by default

entries.d: Displays a vertical pianoroll with event labels. Supports all the same options as pianoroll.
Renders a pitch circle to visualize frequencies within one octave
Displays a spiral visual.
p: Object containing all the optional following parameters as key value pairs:
controls the rotations per cycle ratio, where 1 = 1 cycle / 360 degrees
style of line ends: butt (default), round, square
number of rotations before spiral starts (default 3)
color of playhead, defaults to white
length of playhead in rotations, defaults to 0.02
thickness of playheadrotations, defaults to thickness
steadyness of spiral vs playhead. 1 = spiral doesn't move, playhead does.
color of active segment. defaults to foreground of theme
color of inactive segments. defaults to gutterForeground of theme
wether or not to colorize inactive segments, defaults to 0
wether or not past and future should fade out. defaults to 1
wether or not the spiral should be logarithmic. defaults to 0

entries.d: Change the pitch of each value by the given amount. Expects numbers or note strings as values. The amount can be given as a number of semitones or as a string in interval short notation. If you don't care about enharmonic correctness, just use numbers. Otherwise, pass the interval of the form: ST where S is the degree number and T the type of interval with M = major m = minor P = perfect A = augmented d = diminished Examples intervals: 1P = unison 3M = major third 3m = minor third 4P = perfect fourth 4A = augmented fourth 5P = perfect fifth 5d = diminished fifth
p: Either number of semitones or interval string.

entries.d: Transposes notes inside the scale by the number of steps. Expected to be called on a Pattern which already has a {@link Pattern#scale}
p: number of steps inside the scale

entries.d: Turns numbers into notes in the scale (zero indexed) or quantizes notes to a scale. When describing notes via numbers, note that negative numbers can be used to wrap backwards in the scale as well as sharps or flats to produce notes outside of the scale. Also sets scale for other scale operations, like {@link Pattern#scaleTranspose}. A scale consists of a root note (e.g. c4, c, f#, bb4) followed by semicolon (':') and then a scale type. The scale name must be written without spaces (because it would be interpreted as a multi-step pattern otherwise). If your scale name includes spaces, replace them with colons. The root note defaults to octave 3, if no octave number is given.

entries.d: Maps the chords of the incoming pattern to root notes in the given octave.

Turns chord symbols into voicings. You can use the following control params: chord: Note, followed by chord symbol, e.g. C Am G7 Bb^7 dict: voicing dictionary to use, falls back to default dictionary anchor: the note that is used to align the chord mode: how the voicing is aligned to the anchor below: top note <= anchor duck: top note <= anchor, anchor excluded above: bottom note >= anchor offset: whole number that shifts the voicing up or down to the next voicing n: if set, the voicing is played like a scale. Overshooting numbers will be octaved All of the above controls are optional, except chord. If you pass a pattern of strings to voicing, they will be interpreted as chords.
